main.title: Howe's sewing-machine patent
main.summary: Elias Howe received his US sewing-machine patent on 10 September 1846. Mechanising the joining of fabric with thread helped transform clothing production during the Industrial Revolution.

cards.heading: Howe's sewing-machine patent
cards.text:
Elias Howe received his US sewing-machine patent on 10 September 1846. Mechanising the joining of fabric with thread helped transform clothing production during the Industrial Revolution.

A sewing machine is a machine used to sew fabric and materials together with thread. Sewing machines were invented during the first Industrial Revolution to decrease the amount of manual sewing work performed in clothing companies. Since the invention of the first sewing machine, generally considered to have been the work of Englishman Thomas Saint in 1790, the sewing machine has greatly improved the efficiency and productivity of the clothing industry.

Home sewing machines are designed for one person to sew individual items while using a single stitch type at a time. In a modern sewing machine, the process of stitching has been automated, so that the fabric easily glides in and out of the machine. Early sewing machines were powered by either constantly turning a flywheel handle or with a foot-operated treadle mechanism. Electrically-powered machines were later introduced.

main.title: Foucault pendulum
main.summary: The Foucault pendulum or Foucault's pendulum is a simple device named after French physicist Léon Foucault, conceived as an experiment to demonstrate the Earth's rotation.

cards.heading: Foucault pendulum
cards.text:
The Foucault pendulum or Foucault's pendulum is a simple device named after French physicist Léon Foucault, conceived as an experiment to demonstrate the Earth's rotation. If a long and heavy pendulum suspended from the high roof above a circular area is monitored over an extended period of time, its plane of oscillation appears to change spontaneously as the Earth makes its 24-hourly rotation. This effect is greatest at the poles and diminishes with lower latitude until it no longer exists at Earth's equator.

Foucault introduced his pendulum in 1851 in the first experiment to give simple, direct evidence of the Earth's rotation, which he further demonstrated in 1852 with a gyroscope experiment. Foucault pendulums have become popular in science museums and universities.

main.title: Great Exhibition
main.summary: London's Great Exhibition brought industry and culture into the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park in 1851.

cards.heading: Great Exhibition
cards.text: London's Great Exhibition opened in Hyde Park on 1 May 1851 and continued until 15 October. Henry Cole and Prince Albert organised an international display of industry and culture inside the temporary Crystal Palace. Machinery, manufactured goods and inventions brought different kinds of work before the same public. Michael Faraday helped plan and judge exhibits, while visitors included Charles Darwin, Charles Dickens and Charlotte Brontë. Even practical facilities attracted attention: George Jennings's public flush toilets were among the innovations presented. The event began a series of world's fairs that became a prominent feature of nineteenth-century public life.

main.title: Otis establishes his elevator company
main.summary: Elisha Otis established his elevator company in 1853. His safety mechanism, developed the previous year, locked an elevator car in place if its hoisting rope failed.

cards.heading: Otis establishes his elevator company
cards.text: Elisha Otis established his elevator company in 1853. His safety mechanism, developed the previous year, locked an elevator car in place if its hoisting rope failed. This development became central to a business that expanded from elevators into escalators and moving walkways. The Otis Elevator Company was acquired by United Technologies in 1976 and became independent again in April 2020.

main.title: Bessemer process
main.summary: The Bessemer process was the first inexpensive industrial process for the mass production of steel from molten pig iron before the development of the open hearth furnace.

cards.heading: Bessemer process
cards.text:
The Bessemer process was the first inexpensive industrial process for the mass production of steel from molten pig iron before the development of the open hearth furnace. The key principle is removal of impurities and undesired elements, primarily excess carbon, contained in the pig iron by oxidation with air being blown through the molten iron. Oxidation of the excess carbon also raises the temperature of the iron mass and keeps it molten.

As virtually all the pig iron carbon is removed by the converter, carbon must be added at the end of the process to create steel. 0.25% carbon content is a typical value for low carbon steel which is used in construction and other low-stress applications. 

The modern process is named after its inventor, the Englishman Henry Bessemer, who took out a patent on the process in 1856. The process was said to have been discovered independently in 1851 by the American inventor William Kelly, though the claim is controversial.

main.title: Transatlantic telegraph cable
main.summary: Transatlantic telegraph cables are undersea cables running under the Atlantic Ocean which were used for telegraph communications.

cards.heading: Transatlantic telegraph cable
cards.text: The first transatlantic telegraph cable carried official messages on 16 August 1858, linking Ireland with Newfoundland. Cyrus West Field's Atlantic Telegraph Company had begun the project in 1854. Queen Victoria's message of congratulations to President James Buchanan demonstrated the possibility of communication between the continents, but transmission was slow and signal quality soon deteriorated. After three weeks, excessive voltage applied during attempts to improve operation destroyed the connection. Manufacturing and handling problems also contributed to its vulnerability. The brief success showed what an undersea link could achieve, while its failure damaged confidence and delayed another attempt.

main.title: On the Origin of Species
main.summary: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species on 24 November 1859, presenting a scientific explanation of how populations change over generations through natural selection.

cards.heading: On the Origin of Species
cards.text: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species on 24 November 1859, presenting a scientific explanation of how populations change over generations through natural selection. He drew on observations from the Beagle voyage, later research, correspondence and experiments to argue that life's diversity arose through common descent and branching evolution. The book entered an existing debate about biological change, but brought a substantial body of evidence into a single account. It became a foundation of evolutionary biology and challenged scientific institutions closely tied to the Church of England.

main.title: Lenoir's gas engine
main.summary: Etienne Lenoir produced a gas-fired internal combustion engine in 1860.

cards.heading: Lenoir's gas engine
cards.text: Etienne Lenoir produced a gas-fired internal combustion engine in 1860. Burning fuel inside a chamber created hot, expanding gases that pushed the engine's moving parts, converting chemical energy into mechanical work. Keeping combustion within the engine opened a route towards machines used in industry and transport. Other designs followed, including Nicolaus Otto's engine of 1876. The principle would take several forms, from familiar piston engines to turbines and rotary engines, each using the pressure of combustion to produce motion.

main.title: American Civil War
main.summary: The American Civil War began on 12 April 1861 when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in South Carolina.

cards.heading: American Civil War
cards.text: The American Civil War began on 12 April 1861 when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in South Carolina. Southern states had seceded after Abraham Lincoln's election, seeking to preserve slavery against its growing political opposition. Their Confederacy fought the Union through a war that lasted until 1865. Union victory brought the Confederacy's dissolution and the national abolition of slavery, freeing four million African Americans. The conflict turned decades of argument over slavery and its expansion into a struggle over the country's political future.
